 Diwali 2026 Calendar: Check All 7 Festival Dates, Rituals and Significance of Each Day
 Diwali 2026 celebrations will begin on November 5 with Govatsa Dwadashi and conclude on November 11 with Bhai Dooj. From Dhanteras and Kali Chaudas to Lakshmi Puja and Govardhan Puja, here is the complete seven-day festival calendar, along with the significance of each day.
 Parthana Bora 
 01 Nov 2026 
 17:07
 IST Follow Us
 New Update Diwali 2026 
 Diwali,  also known as Deepawali, is one of the most important Hindu festivals celebrated across India. Symbolising the victory of light over darkness and good over evil, the festival brings families together for prayers, traditional rituals, gift exchanges and celebrations. 
 Although Diwali is traditionally observed as a five-day festival in many parts of the country, regional customs and variations in the Hindu calendar extend the celebrations. In 2026, the festivities listed in the seven-day calendar will begin on November 5 and conclude on November 11, with the main Diwali and Lakshmi Puja celebrations scheduled for November 8.  
 Diwali 2026: Complete 7-Day Calendar and Festival Dates 
 The seven-day Deepawali calendar includes several religious observances, each carrying its own traditions and significance. Here is the day-wise schedule of the celebrations, including the important festivals and their dates.

 DAY 
 FESTIVAL AND OBSERVANCES

 Thursday Govatsa Dwadashi, Vasu Baras
 November 6, 2026 Friday Dhanteras, Dhantrayodashi, Dhanvantari Trayodashi, Yama Deepam

 Diwali 2026: Significance of Each Day 
 November 5: Govatsa Dwadashi 
 The Diwali festivities begin with Govatsa Dwadashi, also known as Vasu Baras in Maharashtra. The occasion is dedicated to the worship of cows and their calves, which are considered sacred in Hindu traditions. 
 Devotees offer prayers to cows and express gratitude for their contribution to agriculture and everyday life. The observance also reflects the cultural and religious importance of cattle in traditional Hindu households. 
 November 6: Dhanteras 
 Dhanteras, also called Dhantrayodashi, is one of the most significant occasions associated with Diwali. The day is considered auspicious for purchasing gold, silver, utensils and other valuable items, as these are traditionally believed to bring prosperity and good fortune. 
 Goddess Lakshmi and Lord Dhanvantari are worshipped on this day for wealth, prosperity and good health. Many households also observe Yama Deepam by lighting an oil lamp in honour of Yama, the Hindu god of death, seeking protection and well-being for family members. 
 November 7: Kali Chaudas 
 Kali Chaudas is observed in several regional traditions as part of the Diwali celebrations. Also associated with Narak Chaturdashi in certain calendars, the day is dedicated to prayers to Goddess Kali and Lord Hanuman. 
 Devotees perform religious rituals seeking protection from negative forces and the removal of evil influences. The observance carries particular significance in parts of western India. 
 November 8: Narak Chaturdashi and Lakshmi Puja 
 November 8 marks the main Diwali celebrations in the 2026 calendar. The day is also associated with Narak Chaturdashi and Tamil Deepavali. 
 Homes are decorated with colourful rangoli, flowers and traditional earthen lamps. Families wear new clothes, exchange gifts and gather for evening prayers. 
 Lakshmi Puja remains the central ritual of the day, with devotees worshipping Goddess Lakshmi for wealth, prosperity and happiness. Lord Ganesha is worshipped alongside her, as he is believed to bring wisdom, success and remove obstacles. 
 Kali Puja is also observed on this occasion in several parts of India, particularly in West Bengal. Meanwhile, business communities perform traditional rituals such as Chopda Puja and Sharda Puja, seeking success and prosperity in their professional activities. 
 November 9: Diwali Snan and Devpuja 
 The day following the main Diwali celebrations is observed as Diwali Snan and Devpuja in the calendar. 
 Devotees follow traditional bathing rituals and offer prayers to deities as part of their religious observances. The customs associated with the day differ across regions, depending on local traditions and the Hindu calendar. 
 November 10: Govardhan Puja 
 Govardhan Puja, also known as Annakut, is celebrated in many parts of India following Diwali. The festival commemorates the legend of Lord Krishna lifting Govardhan Hill to protect the people of Vrindavan from torrential rainfall sent by Lord Indra. 
 Devotees prepare a variety of food items and arrange them as Annakut offerings before Lord Krishna. Special prayers and rituals are performed in temples and households. 
 The occasion is also observed as Bali Pratipada in several Hindu traditions. In Gujarat, the day marks the beginning of the Gujarati New Year and is celebrated with prayers and festive gatherings. 
 November 11: Bhai Dooj 
 Bhai Dooj, also known as Bhau Beej and Yama Dwitiya, marks the conclusion of the seven-day Diwali calendar. 
 The festival celebrates the bond between brothers and sisters. Sisters apply tilak on their brothers' foreheads and pray for their long lives, happiness and well-being. Brothers, in return, offer gifts and reaffirm their love and support. 
 The occasion highlights the importance of family relationships and brings the Diwali festivities to a traditional close. 
 Why Is Goddess Lakshmi Worshipped During Diwali? 
 Goddess Lakshmi is revered in Hinduism as the deity of wealth, prosperity and abundance. Her worship holds special importance during Diwali, particularly on the Amavasya, or new Moon day, when Lakshmi Puja is performed. 
 According to Hindu traditions, devotees clean and decorate their homes before the festival and light diyas to welcome Goddess Lakshmi. Families offer prayers seeking financial stability, happiness and good fortune. 
 Lord Ganesha is also worshipped alongside Goddess Lakshmi. Devotees seek his blessings for wisdom, success and the removal of obstacles in their lives. 
 The tradition extends to business establishments, where traders and shopkeepers organise special prayers at their workplaces. Account books, pens and inkpots are worshipped as part of traditional rituals, reflecting the importance of knowledge, financial discipline and prosperity. 
 Diwali Lakshmi Puja 2026: Why Is Pradosh Kaal Important? 
 The timing of Lakshmi Puja holds considerable importance in Hindu traditions. The preferred period for performing Diwali prayers is during Pradosh Kaal, which begins after sunset. 
 The date of Diwali is determined by the Amavasya Tithi, or new Moon lunar phase, with particular importance given to its presence during the evening Pradosh period. 
 Pradosh Kaal is traditionally considered auspicious for worship and religious rituals. Even when the Amavasya Tithi overlaps with this period for a limited duration, the corresponding Lakshmi Puja Muhurat is regarded as significant. 
 Since the timing of religious observances may vary depending on geographical location and regional panchang calculations, devotees are advised to check their local Hindu calendar for the precise Lakshmi Puja Muhurat and other festival timings. 
 Conclusion 
 Diwali is more than a festival of lights, with each day of the celebrations reflecting different aspects of Hindu traditions, devotion and family relationships. From worshipping cows on Govatsa Dwadashi and seeking prosperity on Dhanteras to celebrating the bond between siblings on Bhai Dooj, the seven-day calendar brings together a range of religious and cultural observances. 
 As Diwali 2026 approaches, these celebrations will once again bring families and communities together through prayers, traditional customs and festive gatherings across the country.
